utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam registrar. Madam Usher, on the assumption the Defence is ready to continue the cross-examination, I would like to ask you to escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for the witness to come in I do have a hard copy of our spreadsheet which has the footnotes from 1 to 400 and whatever, with a cross-reference to what the master tab number is where that document is found. If I could hand that up. I've already provided two copies to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you could do that without doing all the work again or...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. We had to hide some columns, but we have that for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Provide them to the registrar, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The footnote number appears on the far left column, and I think the Court will be able to follow the rest of it easily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson. The same procedure as the last few days. I'd like to remind you, perhaps unnecessarily, but I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for that document from Mr. Hannis. I'm going to mark it Variant C. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson. Ms. Hanson, we were looking - well, I think we were - at paragraph 38 of your report. Do you have your report in front of you again this morning?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. Yes, I found paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in particular a certain sentence, the second sentence, it's not a long paragraph: "In that capacity, he apparently signed for Karadzic," he being Mr. Krajisnik, "at least two Presidency documents dealing with appointments of commissioners." And Mr. Hannis before court this morning showed me another one which I understood to be in the same category.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And for information of the witness and the Court, it is presentation tab 69 which we showed to Defence counsel and he discussed with his client this morning and I understand it appears to be his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well on the basis of the photocopy shown to Mr. Krajisnik, he doesn't as things stand at the moment have any dispute as to that, but I think he has made a slight reservation that he has only seen a photocopy at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Ms. Hanson, I'm going to proceed on the footing that that is an extra -- an example, but it is just an extra example. The -- when you describe in your report Mr. Krajisnik as signing in that capacity, what is the basis of your use of that phrase "in that capacity"?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a member of the Presidency and tying it to the fact that he was named as the member of the Presidency given the task of the question of commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The documents were -- in the first place the person who was to sign the document and that's shown the typed signature was Dr. Karadzic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in some sense Mr. Krajisnik was signing on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And not in his own specific capacity?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Presidency minutes of the 6th of July where Mr. Krajisnik is tasked as the member of the Presidency for the question of commissioners, it is -- the context appears to be dividing up the tasks which until now Mr. Karadzic as the president of the Presidency has -- the decision is in the context of replacing -- of when Mr. -- Mr. Karadzic can't do it all. If I can see -- or if you recall those government minutes, that's the context of agenda item 4. What we do when Mr. Karadzic isn't there and -- but apparently they seem to be dividing up various tasks. But all Presidency documents are type-signed -- to the best of my recollection, Presidency decisions and such are type-signed by Karadzic as president of the Presidency. That's my general understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I suppose what it is is this, Ms. Hanson, are you in fact relying upon Mr. Krajisnik's signature of those documents as some reinforcement or strengthening of his role as the member of the Presidency responsible for the work of the republican commissioners?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take those signatures as indication that he did -- within the Presidency he did conduct some affairs of the Presidency related to the republican commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't suggest, though, do you, that for example if Dr. Karadzic being unavailable and Mr. Krajisnik had been unavailable, that there would have then been any problem about, for example, Ms. Plavsic signing that document -- Mrs. Plavsic, I mean.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know much about the rules of the procedure of the Presidency, and I don't know much about other signatures -- other people's signatures on other Presidency documents. I focused on the Presidency documents relevant to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you check to see whether any other documents apparently coming from Dr. Karadzic were signed by any other member of the Presidency on his behalf in a similar manner?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not check to see that as a particular issue, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's move on to paragraph 43 of your report. You say in the second sentence: "As members of the Presidency, both Krajisnik and Plavsic visited Crisis Staffs and received reports from them on the situation in critical municipalities." Now, of course we're agreed, aren't we, Ms. Hanson, that this report was prepared at a time when one of the indictees still before the court and this trial on this indictment was Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact it's the -- you only give one example, don't you, of Dr. -- of Mr. Krajisnik visiting a Crisis Staff and receiving a report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this report I give that one example. I have given other examples in my presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you pick the best example here for your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I found to be the best example at the time of the documents I had available then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you suggest that one of your other examples is a better example?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intercepts that I presented in my presentation plan are also good examples I feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's look at this one then. This is a visit by Mr. Krajisnik to Ilijas, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything apart what can be seen on the documents about the circumstances of Mr. Krajisnik's visit to Ilijas on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this occasion, no, I do not know more than that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the way in which the Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik recognised St. Vitus Day that year?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't know anything, therefore, and haven't heard anything about different people, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik included, in the broad SDS leadership going to various different places to mark and honour that day?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that it was named as the -- a holiday for the army, I believe a day of particular significance for the army. And I believe that the Bosnian Serb leadership did send -- various members of the leadership did attend or take part in some such markings of the day, but in detail I'm not aware of the details of who went where.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what you have seen is consistent with the suggestion that I put to you, that it was that day was much more of a ceremonial day than a business day?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I have indicates that it combined both ceremony and business because they talk about the -- I don't have the document in front of me, but as I recall they talk about the larger celebration and some speeches and then they specifically name -- mention that the delegation visited the Crisis Staff and was briefed on the events on the ground. And they don't describe it as part of -- they specified it as different from the larger speeches given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. You recall that in the footnote where the delegation was briefed on the situation in the field, which is gained, and we do see that in writing, that's gained from the report or note coming from the people in Ilijas, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew that from the report. The report -- the document, yes, appears to stem from Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They refer to it themselves as a short visit, don't they?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document in front of me but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you can take that from me, Ms. Hanson, that it does say that. That's easily checkable. We won't dwell and spend time on it. There's nothing more that you know about that visit than what we see in that document then, is there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That document is my -- the source I use here for that. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have seen a newspaper article talk -- and I'm not sure about this, talking in general terms about those kind of St. Vitus Day celebrations. But this is what I use. I'm not relying on anything beyond it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your report says that both Mr. Krajisnik and Mrs. Plavsic visited Crisis Staffs and received reports on them and situations in critical municipalities. So you are classifying, are you, Ilijas for these purposes as a critical municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what is it -- what are the features of Ilijas that made it a critical municipality on the 28th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not mean that it was specifically critical on that day, but it was one of the municipalities in the Sarajevo region and as we know that one of the strategy objectives of the Bosnian Serbs was control of part of Sarajevo. Ilijas was the scene of some considerable fighting, and I believe there were some important industries located there, but there were industries throughout the wider Sarajevo region. So I'm not exactly sure which ones were located there. But as a Sarajevo municipality and the scene of fighting, I would call it critical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And are you in your report here in saying that, are you drawing the conclusion that the reason for Mr. Krajisnik visiting Ilijas was that it was in some sense a critical municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not say that that was the reason he visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Wouldn't it have been better to have made that clear then in your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that as misleading here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you don't agree that that sentence of your report contains the very clear implication that the visits you refer to by Mr. Krajisnik and Mrs. Plavsic were made to municipalities because they were critical?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mean to tie the actual visit to the determination of whether the municipality was critical or not. We see from the telephone intercepts that when municipalities have a crisis or have something critical to report that on at least two occasions those Crisis Staffs did make contact with Krajisnik. But this sentence here -- I'm -- if you could repeat your -- or I'll just read it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I can --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. I'm not used to reading the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, no, understood.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the sentence could be read in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I did not make it explicit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We confirm you don't now mean it that way?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't mean it that way. I agree it could be read that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact you have not seen, have you, from the material you've examined any -- well, in the first place any pattern of Mr. Krajisnik visiting critical municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not of him visiting those municipalities, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You haven't seen any pattern of him having contact with critical municipalities, have you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated in my presentation, he did receive phone calls from Crisis Staffs in municipalities and through the Assembly he was informed as the Assembly deputies spoke of important events in their municipalities. So although he was not visiting the municipalities in question, he was hearing about events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What is the furthest municipality from Sarajevo where you have been able to identify any such contact or report of any nature with or to Mr. Krajisnik relating to the work of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the Assembly we have reports from Brcko which is on the northern border with Croatia. We have reports from Kljuc and Krupa which are fairly close to the north-west border --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't wish to talk over you, but I can stop you and shorten there. If you're talking about what appears in the Assembly session, then you have immediately brought us right up to the border.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that's as far as one can get. So I will then specifically exclude that and confine my question, please, to Mr. Krajisnik himself. So that you referred to intercepts, you've referred specifically to this visit. So that's what I'm talking about. I'm talking about the category of direct contacts with or reports to Mr. Krajisnik. And so my question is: What is the furthest municipality from Sarajevo in relation to which you have been able to identify any sort of contact or report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the discussion in the Assembly on commissioners, Mr. Krajisnik says he was aware of the work of the commissioners, and the commissioners he names were sent to I believe Foca and Herzegovina but I don't know which municipalities in Herzegovina specifically. Maksimovic was sent to Trebinje and Mr. Krajisnik indicates he was aware of the work of Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, are you able to read on the screen in front of you the question which I just put to you. It's about eight lines, starting --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, identify any further contact or report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you just re-read that question and then tell the Trial Chamber whether the answer you've just given is the best answer you're able to give to that question.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: "What is the furthest municipality from Sarajevo in relation to which you've been able to identify any sort of contact or report" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, you need to read the whole question in order to understand what it is I was asking.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. "Oh, specifically exclude that" -- "I will then specifically exclude that and confine my question, please, to Mr. Krajisnik himself. So that you've referred to intercepts, you've referred specifically to this visit. So this is what I'm talking about, I'm talking about the category of direct contacts with or reports to Mr. Krajisnik. And so my question is: What is the furthest municipality from Sarajevo in relation to which you've been able to identify any sort of contact or report?" So it -- excluding the Assembly sessions, the contacts that I have seen are from Sarajevo-area municipalities, as to whether Vogosca or Ilijas is further away from where Mr. Krajisnik was, I would have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Vogosca is. But the -- Ms. Hanson, you know that Mr. Krajisnik is from Sarajevo, do you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Sarajevo area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you know that Ilijas is extremely near to where Mr. Krajisnik lived at the time and indeed to where he was born?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where he was born. But, yes, I know Ilijas is very close to where he lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is it consistent with all material you've seen that on St. Vitus Day in 1992 Mr. Krajisnik was going somewhere near to where he lived for the purpose of that day?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question at this moment, Ms. Hanson. Some questions were asked about the critical situation in municipalities. If you would include footnote 83 in your assessment, would that say something about the situation later in June or the situation in Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It indicates the president of the Ilijas Crisis Staff is describing the situation as critical and asking for assistance. If I may make one clarification about that document in that footnote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies. The document as indicated there is not exactly -- doesn't say what I claim because there were two documents side by side, one after another, very similar, and the second one got dropped off. I have a copy of it to show the Court that -- how the error crept in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well perhaps, Mr. Hannis, we could give this a follow-up in the further examination? So Mr. Hannis will ask you for further clarification --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My apologies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course the Chamber is always -- has an open ear and eye for whatever adjustment is necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you have the report in front of you anyhow, could I draw your extension to footnote 68 under the heading SAOs --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You give what seems to be two examples. "The Crisis Staff of SAO Birac declared a state of war on the territory." That's the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then on the bottom of the page, last two lines, with a different ERN number, it reads: "SAO Birac Crisis Staff declares a state of war on the basis of..." Is that the same document? Is that the same example, or are these -- unfortunately, I now see that I should have brought binders 5 and 8 to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that one of the documents is a document of the Bratunac Crisis Staff citing the Salvirac [phoen] decision. I would have to check, but they are not the same document to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the description is so similar and although if perhaps you could check that during the next break whether we are talking about one example or two examples.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question to ask. Ms. Hanson. Could you on the basis of the documents that you have consulted or used, could you actually replace this visit of Mr. Krajisnik on June the 28th of 1992 for which he was briefed on the situation in the field. What is the situation -- the situation at the particular time in region of Ilijas? I'm going to be very specific. Is this situation a situation in which people live in peace or there is no war; or is it -- the situation in which they were in detention -- the place in which there are detention centres for civilians? Or any abuses committed? Does this appear from the documents you have looked at or does it not appear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On my basis of the general understanding of the war, I would say that Ilijas was a front line municipality, being a Sarajevo municipality. It was an area in which there were -- it was in or near the front line of the war. As far as detention centres and so on, I did not look into that specifically for that matter, of what abuses or other such events might be going on in Ilijas at this time. But it was I believe a scene of fighting because the war was there, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- may I just comment as a matter of information. As indicated by Mr. Hannis the other day, we have three, I think it is, witnesses coming up in relation to Ilijas in the last few days before the short Easter break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This reminds me of another matter, Mr. Stewart. I'm asking, yesterday you were talking about recess. Were you referring to the Easter recess or the Easter break or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believed it was clear from the context, but I did specifically confirm to Ms. Philpott, that I was referring -- it's a bit of a misnomer, I must say, but I was referring to the Easter break which I classified in my mind as recess, because even a couple of days is at least some relief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should have asked her first because I asked her to -- to verify that. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Even I wouldn't need four months to deal with that point about Mr. Bjelobrk, Your Honour. Well, not yet anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, a slight interjection then arising out of what you've just said. Coincidentally, in effect, in connection with His Honour Judge Orie's question, you informed the Trial Chamber very helpfully that there was in fact an error in relation to footnote 83 and the document didn't support it. And I therefore ask whether there are other such errors and discrepancies which you have been able to identify in the course of your work and your evidence, which like that one have not been expressly brought yet to the attention of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the only one I have found so far, other than the changes made in my corrigendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it is a complete coincidence that His Honour's question threw up that particular error?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I have -- because that error came to my attention when I was preparing and I wanted to -- I brought a copy just to be prepared to indicate how the error arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I feel the Trial Chamber will, with respect, endorse this, but may I invite you that at any point if you do yourself identify any error or need for correction for your report that it is brought immediately or as soon as convenient to the attention of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May we turn then -- the way I'm going to do it, with respect, Your Honour, is I have -- of course, we all have transcripts of your evidence so far, Ms. Hanson, your recorded -- by the way, may I ask you, have you had an opportunity of reviewing the daily transcripts yourself of your evidence as we've been going along?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not reviewed them -- reviewed that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- I'm working from the daily transcripts which do not have the continuous numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hope, will understand it's not really practical to do it that way, and we have to work immediately on the daily transcripts we get, and each start at number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- I want to look first, please, at what is found on Wednesday -- and they're relatively short passages, Ms. Hanson, and you're familiar with this material anyway. So what I'm actually going to do is just remind you of the point. If we do at any stage get into difficulty about it and you feel that you really must see the material in question, then of course please don't hesitate to say so. The -- you referred to deny intercept on -- this was on Wednesday, the 2nd of March, and the transcript reference for everybody's benefit is page 59. And it relates to an intercept of a telephone conversation between Mr. Jovan Tinto and Mr. Krajisnik on the 3rd of April, 1992. And I expect you're pretty familiar and that's pretty firmly in your mind, Ms. Hanson, is it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And it went -- I'm not going to just read once again into the record the whole thing. I'm just going to concentrate, it was in a nutshell -- Mr. Tintor was talking about Muslims coming from Kovilja Glava [phoen], they are on their way towards Gravista, and he said: "Please, it's my duty to inform you," he's talking to Mr. Krajisnik, "of what's going on." And then he referred to -- he said he was calling from the headquarters. He said he had just spoken with Rajko. Do you know or accept that Rajko there was Rajko Kopravica?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems a logical conclusion, but I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't know for sure --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. You have no reason to doubt that that suggestion --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then Mr. Krajisnik is saying a few lines later on. He says: "Well, best man," he calls him, "we need to try everything to calm the situation down." And then Mr. Mandzic has been there according to Mr. Tintor. Mr. Krajisnik says: "Very important to keep peace." And then Tintor says: "Yes, they're on the move, best man." And Mr. Krajisnik says: "I don't think they are." And it ends up with Mr. Krajisnik saying: "Yeah, because there's panic. You check this. All right. There may be something going on. You need to check on this panic." Tintor: "Yes." Mr. Krajisnik: "Check it and let me know. I'll be here." Ms. Hanson, do you know that Mr. Tintor and Mr. Krajisnik at that time knew each other very well personally?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used the personal form of address in this conversation, the informal. They call each other "best man," and in Jovan Tintor's interview -- I didn't play that part but I did look at his entire interview. He says that he knew Krajisnik quite well from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But you don't know more than that then?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were both on the Main Board, but how -- that doesn't necessarily mean intimate friends. But from the phone conversation alone it's clear that they know each other well, because as I said they use the informal address.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there's nothing -- from what you see, nothing inconsistent from the proposition that they actually knew each other very well personally and were really close?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing inconsistent with that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And this is Goska, Lagoska [phoen] we're talking again, aren't we, about somewhere which is near to where Mr. Krajisnik lives and is based?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is what you've seen then inconsistent with this being -- obviously it's to do with what's happening, Ms. Hanson, I'm not suggesting that, but consistent with it being more in the nature of a personal approach to somebody important to Mr. Krajisnik, somebody important who Mr. Tintor knew well to tell him about the situation, rather than a formal report to Mr. Krajisnik in some capacity, official capacity, in relation to the work of the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's both because he -- Tintor does say, "It is my duty to inform you." So I see both purposes to this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is the -- we may have to look at the document for this, but the -- do you recall specifically what is the precise sense of the B/C/S or would you need to see the document as well?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to see the document to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I think perhaps that would be a good idea then. It's master tab 406. Yes, it's the B/C/S which I'm inviting you to have, Ms. Hanson. I'd just like you to read -- I'll just make it clear, Ms. Hanson, at this point I'm not challenging you. I just would invite you to read that bit of the B/C/S so that we can have it interpreted as we go. So I suggest that you start at "I think a conflict would break out" or the B/C/S equivalent of that, that's Mr. Tintor, just Mr. Krajisnik says, "Yeah."

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tintor says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think the interpreter did not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Krajisnik: "Please it is my duty to inform you what is happening at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may just address the interpreter. It seems that you -- initial understanding -- whatever initial misunderstanding, the interpreters now seem to have understood the witness perfectly well. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not the first sentence I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What, about the -- let's just do it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour. Thank you. I'm obliged for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tintor: "I think that it's going to blast up there." Krajisnik: "Yeah." Tintor: "Please, it is my duty to inform you what at this moment."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Ms. Hanson, you're getting -- from that you attach quite some significance to that phraseology, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it a telling phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you'll link together, just to confirm the understanding, you link together the fact that Mr. Tintor is the head of the Vogosca Crisis Staff, with him saying it's his duty to inform Mr. Krajisnik, and then there's nothing else at that point, is there, 3rd of April, 1992, apart from whatever positions Mr. Krajisnik held at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Noting simply that Tintor says he's calling from the Vogosca "shtab," [phoen] staff, is another indication of -- is something else I tie to that phrase. But in -- I do not claim that this is a formal report but that as Tintor himself indicated in his interview he had other forms of communicating with Krajisnik and the Bosnian Serb leadership. This is indication, at a minimum, of a head of a Crisis Staff and member of the Main Board communicating to Krajisnik about events on the ground, and that is how I represented it in my presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the duty that is referred to then and which you attach some significance to, what was the basis of that duty then? What -- the position of Mr. Tintor, that's clear, the head of the Crisis Staff; we needn't debate that. So that's one side. And then Mr. Krajisnik's position and the particular structure which made it Mr. Tintor's duty to report this to -- relate it to Mr. Krajisnik, what do you say that was?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not say that it was any specific position because at this point the only normative document for Crisis Staff is the 19th December instructions, the instructions we see coming out later this month. April do say that Crisis Staffs are -- have a link to the republican organs. In this I think it indicative of the overlap at the highest level of a number of different positions, both in the SDS and the Assembly and the Bosnian Serb organs as we discussed when we first presented this intercept. Tintor says at the beginning he's calling the Speaker, but I don't know that means he's calling him because he is Speaker of the Assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I make a suggestion to you there, Ms. Hanson, he's got the telephone at the Assembly where Mr. Krajisnik works. So he's simply saying who he wants to get through to.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is how I explained it when we first introduced this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So there's no special significance there. That doesn't carry the matter any further than the fact that he wanted to speak to Mr. Krajisnik, does it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. So then you -- well, it's this, isn't it, that this is before -- of course before the meeting of the 6th of July, 1992, obviously?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was April. We see that. Mr. Krajisnik -- you have not identified any specific position that Mr. Krajisnik held at that time in relation to Crisis Staffs, specific?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the Main Board, and the 19th December instructions bear the letterhead of the Main Board of the SDS. And as I indicate in my report, it was -- the Crisis Staffs looked to the Bosnian Serb leadership in general terms and saw themselves as part of this system now being set up, the state system now being set up, the system that arose from the SDS party. So as I indicated in my report there, it's the overlap of these organs that lead to some imprecision on the ground but they certainly saw themselves -- these municipal bodies certainly saw themselves as part of the system now at this point being created.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Hanson, on the basis my question included the word "specific" and your answer included the word "general." We'll move on then to this question which is: On the basis of what you've seen as at the beginning of April 1992, so far as there was a specific duty on Mr. Tintor to make such reports, it would have been a duty to make them to Dr. Koljevic, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why Mr. -- Dr. Koljevic specifically at the beginning of April -- as I said in my report, this is the time when Crisis Staffs begin to emerge from the secrecy of being party organs to more public governmental roles and certainly the 3rd of April is still a transient time, as we saw on the 1st of April, the Bijeljina Crisis Staff reports to the SDS Main Board. In terms of Mr. Koljevic's position in the Presidency, I would have to check -- I don't know offhand when the Presidency as that started meeting, but I don't believe -- pardon me, but I don't believe the 3rd of April there was -- the Presidency was meeting. So in that respect I don't see that he would report to Dr. Koljevic specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you're saying the Presidency was of no particular significance as of that date in this context, are you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure, since I have focused in my preparation on the municipal level and did not commit to memory the details of the republican level. I cannot recall the time at which we see the Presidency as such beginning to meet, and I don't want to speak with any certainty on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The next intercept that you referred to in the same passage of your evidence, that was Wednesday, the 2nd of March, and it was immediately after that one, so it's at the foot of page 61 for the record and reference. You refer to -- and we heard an intercept of -- well, we read anyway, a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Momo Garic on the 21st of April, 1992. You recall that, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Garic had -- it was Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. You summarise it as he's calling Mr. Krajisnik to discuss problems on the ground. And Mr. Krajisnik was saying, Sure, come up, have a meeting. And you say "he's clearly available to Crisis Staff members and interested in the situation on the ground." Do you know that Mr. Garic was also personally close to Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. If I could see the original B/C/S, I could confirm whether he uses the informal form of address, which is a general indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's see that then, shall we. Mr. Hannis is very alert to have that ready for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They appear to use the formal form of address with each other, but they inquire after each other's -- they know each other. They inquire after each other's well being.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And this is -- this of course is local, isn't it, to Mr. Krajisnik? It's Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you have drawn the inference that because Mr. Garic was a member of the Crisis Staff, that shows that Mr. Krajisnik was available to Crisis Staff members; that's the way you've put it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Expressed generally.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hanson, I want to make it clear, not necessarily suggesting, I leave it entirely neutral as to Mr. Krajisnik would have rejected approaches. But we have -- so far what you've identified is Mr. Tintor and Mr. Garic both well-known to Mr. Krajisnik. Do you accept that it is -- one should apply considerable caution to moving from such contacts with people who are well-known to Mr. Krajisnik to some general proposition that he had a function and was available to Crisis Staff members across the board?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that mischaracterises her testimony. She didn't say members across the board. She just said members.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The point is the same if I simply strike, as Mr. Harmon would say, the phrase across the board.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we see from the 19 December instructions, Crisis Staff members were to include Assembly deputies and members of the Main Board. In both those contexts Mr. Krajisnik would know Crisis Staff members. Other members of the Main Board have also been identified as Crisis Staff members in their municipalities. And it is precisely because Crisis Staffs were set up by the SDS, and Mr. Krajisnik was a leader of the SDS and the Assembly he would know Crisis Staff members in a variety of contexts. And similarly Crisis Staff members who wanted to contact the leadership might not think in rigid categories of for this particular issue I contact such a person, but I think that to a large extent they would rely on their pre-existing acquaintances whom they knew in informal channels of communications as well as formal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, embedded in that answer is something which I put to you, which is that of course personal -- in politics, which this was among other things, of course personal contacts are continually used and exploited, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So that what I was suggesting to you was that great caution needs to be applied in inferring from the use of those personal contacts specific formal responsibilities and duties. Do you agree with that as a general proposition?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm looking at your question now that I've learned to use it. The question of specific formal responsibilities and duties. I do not infer from these conversations that we've been discussing that these Crisis Staff members thought that Mr. Krajisnik had in his -- had specific formal responsibilities for those Crisis Staffs. I read it rather that they see him as a member of the leadership of the state, someone to whom they can turn, and someone to whom they should inform of events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you get any impression from the documents you've read and these intercepts that Mr. Krajisnik was more than capable of being a calming influence on the people who came in contact -- had contact with him?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly see that in the Tintor intercept where he is trying to calm Mr. Tintor and saying I don't think there is -- I don't think this calls for panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there is an impression there, isn't there, Ms. Hanson, that Mr. Tintor was panicking?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was alarmed. His voice doesn't sound, I would say, panicked, but he is clearly alarmed about the events on the ground, and Mr. Krajisnik is endeavouring to calm him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So do you get any impression, then, that's what's happening there is what will often happen as a person who is very panicked and wound up will naturally contact somebody that their experience shows is going to calm them and instinctively contact somebody, experience shows, who is likely to calm them down.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reluctant to get into the psychology of the conversation, because once again I return to the phrase "my duty to inform you" he is not just saying, I'm worried, he's informing somebody who he thinks can assist in this situation or who should know about this situation at least. I take it as simply more than calling a friend who would calm him down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, to be -- to try to be fair, Ms. Hanson, I'm not trying to put you in that -- extra role of an expert psychologist; that would be rather unfair. I was simply asking whether you had got that impression from your reading of all the documents.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I certainly see it -- I see that attempt to calm in this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, the next -- I don't want to dwell on that intercept anymore, and we can move on. You also in your evidence, and it's pretty much in the same part of evidence, Wednesday, 2nd March, at page 64 you refer to an Assembly session. It's the May the 12th Assembly session. And you refer to a speech of Mr. Radic's and it's -- the reference is there. And Mr. Radic had said: "At the intervention of the president of the Assembly," Mr. Krajisnik, "we released that Ustasha, that Ivo Stanic whom I had taken prisoner. This is what I regret having done most." And the use of the word "Ustasha" confirms what in fact is the case that Mr. Stanic was Croat.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume from the name Ivo and as you say from the reference to Ustastha. They use Ustasha generally to mean Croats on the enemy side. But, yes, I would take that to mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We see that --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From that statement, from his speech I would logically infer that Ivo Stanic was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what the Defence put to you anyway, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then you said -- you noted here because it's indicating that Radic received a direct intervention -- I'm sorry, received an intervention from the president, from Krajisnik as president of the Assembly, and I'm not suggesting there's any other president referred to here, that is Mr. Krajisnik, and "released the prisoner upon his intervention even though Radic did not want to do it." Ms. Hanson, that's not - and say if you wish to be refreshed with the actual document - but I put to you that's not what Mr. Radic is saying. He's not saying he did not want to do it. He is saying he regretted having done it, which is something quite different, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it's quite different. I inferred his not wanting to do it from his statement of regret. That's, I think, a reasonable inference. I don't -- I don't know how else to read that he regrets having done it unless he is -- I'm -- I don't see -- that's how I make the connection. I think it's justified by his expression, but -- and I don't understand the difference entirely that you're drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, you want to let your son use your car and your son goes out and uses your car, you want to do it, you want him to have it. He smashes it up - my son's never done this - but he smashes it up, you regret the fact that you let him take your car out that night. But it wasn't that you didn't want to do it at the time. Do you understand that simple distinction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if it's of any use to you, you've drawn our attention and the attention of Ms. Hanson to the original text and you see a difference which I can follow and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's this, just to clear this up, Ms. Hanson, the impression given by your evidence then is that Mr. Radic didn't want to do something and that in some way Mr. Krajisnik overrode him.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the differences; you explained it with your analogy. I would say he did something that was against his inclinations, and he did that thing because of Mr. Krajisnik's intervention. But I understand the difference and the Court has --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Hanson, I'm going to put to you very specifically because after all apart from everything I do have instructions from Mr. Krajisnik in relation to certain things, that what happened was that Mr. Radic in no way overrode, that Mr. Krajisnik did use his position to get Mr. Stanic released because Mr. Stanic was a deputy of the Assembly, so he was one of Mr. Krajisnik's colleagues and he did get him released. Do you know -- do you -- what, do you know anything to contradict that, Ms. Hanson, is question number one?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not know anything and that is consistent with what Radic says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then in the same batch of evidence, if you like, that was Wednesday, the 2nd of March then at page 65, you then referred to and gave evidence about an intercept of a conversation between Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik and Mr. Mirko Krajisnik. And you know -- I expect it was expressly recorded somewhere in your evidence, but you know that Mr. Mirko Krajisnik is Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik's brother?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And also that this all relates to one of the Sarajevo municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which is Mr. Krajisnik's own -- his home municipality, if you like. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And there seems a bit of vagueness here on Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik's part about this -- well, I'll just remind you. Momcilo Krajisnik. Now Mr. Krajisnik here: "Okay. Tell me how things are going in Rajlovac. You know ... "Mirko: Which things?" No disrespect; it's just easier that way. "Momcilo: That man from the municipality the one that came recently, the commissioner. Mirko: Yes, yes, he's not there. He said he would be absent two days. I don't know where he is. But apparently he will be here at the meeting tomorrow. Momcilo: Okay." You agree that Mr. Krajisnik doesn't seem to be greatly in the picture about what is going on there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is inquiring about his whereabouts as far as I know or whether he's come or not. So he's trying to learn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: About his --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: About him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And about something happening in his own home municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: From his own brother?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, you're not going to draw any significant inference from that, are you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I draw inference from the fact that he's inquiring about the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what's the date of that? I'm just reminding myself.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's late June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 22nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There was a lot going on then, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not surprising that Mr. Mirko Krajisnik or Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik talk about a little bit more -- I was going to say next week's football match; wrong time of year perhaps.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A talk about cricket would be surprising, but that's another matter. The -- let's then look at what you say about the role of the Assembly and the members of the Assembly. You referred to -- and again, Wednesday, the 2nd of March you referred to -- it's tab -- presentation tab 108 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first perhaps, Mr. Stewart, correct myself. I was referring to the date of tab 120, and only now looking at it a bit better you're referring to tab 119 in the presentation tab binder, which is the 20th of June, so two days before the date I mentioned. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for the -- thank you for that correction, Your Honour. I'm obliged. Excuse me, Your Honour, I'm wondering which is the more convenient reference document here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At -- it's at page 55 of your transcript, Wednesday, the 2nd of March, you referred to presentation tab 108 which is a record or a transcript of the 17th Session of the Serb Assembly on the 26th of July, 1992. And you referred specifically to comments by Mr. Jovo Mijatovic where he said: "It is the MPs," that is the Members of Parliament, "who are to transfer the authority of the republic to the municipalities and from the municipalities here, an indication of their view of the role of assemblymen." That's -- well, that would be a fairly standard uncontroversial view of the role of any Member of Parliament pretty much in any parliament, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Consistent, I think, with the general role of parliament members, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we look -- I would invite you to be given this then, please. This is presentation binder 3, tab 108. Is this something -- may I inquire, I'm sorry, I'm not sure the person to ask for my inquiries. Is this something that can be brought up on the screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And I've just handed it to Ms. Hanson, and the portion you're talking about is highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I check with you the page number. Page 58 of the translation; that's what you've got, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we just scroll up, please, a tiny bit. Thank you. And then back to -- I'm sorry, here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see in the middle of what we've got on the screen now it says "this strong central power." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "This strong central power should also manifest itself in one more issue, and that is the fact that in this moment the Presidency and the government should get extraordinary authorisations in order to be able to act promptly in certain situations. If we need to say more, as most MPs have already noticed a strong central authority should also manifest itself in the status MPs. Everyone has said and our president has repeated several times that an MP represents authority." Again, Ms. Hanson, do you -- the nature of all the research and study you've done over the years, do you agree that generally speaking in parliaments throughout the world, members of that parliament tend to be very jealous of their status very concerned to ensure that their status and authority is properly recognised?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any basis for making a general statement about other parliamentary systems. I would say that parliamentary members do see themselves as having an important role -- they're part of the government, they're part of the authorities, but as far as their jealousness of their role, I don't want to make a statement regarding their jealousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've never seen that as a feature of political life in all your studies over the years?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it, but I'm just reluctant to speak of all parliamentary systems all over the world as you seem to be talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then what it says: "Everyone has said" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stewart, I get the feeling I do not know whether Mr. Krajisnik is able to follow because on the computer evidence screen I've got pages which seem not to be the right ones because I see that the last three digits of the ERN number, the relevant pages, that is page 59 and 60 should be 553 and 554, as I see now 523 on my screen, page 29. And I really have some difficulties in combining them since I would very much appreciate it if Mr. Krajisnik at least has an opportunity to follow on the screen the original B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure, Your Honour. I don't wish -- I don't wish to bring any pressure on Mr. Krajisnik in relation to this. I'm not sure whether he is immediately concerned as he is able to get the B/C/S translation -- interpretation as I am reading it. If he is concerned at this moment, then of course he will say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Concerned or not it is a general concern of the Chamber that Mr. Krajisnik is able to follow if he wants to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed. I am heartily endorsing that, Your Honour. I am suggesting in relation to this specific piece of evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- if he has that opportunity and isn't concerned, then I am not concerned on his behalf right now at this particular point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you may continue and at the same time the OTP will try to follow the general guidelines. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged. But the general point I entirely 100 per cent accept, Your Honour. I do wish Mr. Krajisnik to be able to follow, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then this Mr. Jovo Tovic I think it says, isn't it, has said: "Everyone has said and our president has repeated several times that an MP represents authority. However, an MP is anything but authority. An MP is someone with who every scumbag and low-life can do what they please. This has especially proved at checkpoints where we have single out certain ministers right here. There are checkpoints where we do not know who is appointed for, who controls whom, and not to mention that some MPs cannot pass certain checkpoints and are being mistreated even by legally that authority which now considers itself legally elected. I suggest that the question of status does not reflect as flat rate," that's what's written there, "but rather in certain authority writes and responsibilities of the MPs that they have to undertake in the wartime period. It is the MPs who are to transfer the authority of the republic to the municipalities and from the municipalities here." Now, that last sentence is the highlighted passage, but do you agree, Ms. Hanson, that the picture presented by this particular Assembly member of the situation and the way in which their work is done presents a rather more difficult and complicated picture than simply of people able to perform their duty of transferring authority backwards forwards, republic to municipalities and municipalities to republic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's indicating that -- yes, there is some circumstances or some places in which assemblymen have not been getting the respect that he feels they should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The picture is a lot for difficult than they want it to be, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's describing difficulties, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then on the next page of the same day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just on this same page. Ms. Hanson, I would like you to comment this red highlighted sentence. I do not understand how a member of the Assembly could be in charge of transferring the republic authority, i.e., to represent the republic at the level of municipalities. In the notion that I have of a democratic system, I do believe that the role of the MP is to listen to whatever citizens have to say and expectations and also to transfer decisions made by the Assembly to them. What I do not understand: How the MP should be in charge of transferring the republic authority towards the municipalities. He's not an agent of the republic; he's elected but he's not an agent of the republic such as a district prefect, for instance. I don't understand this sentence. Could you explain it for me, please. I'd like to take the floor again. So what it would mean, if I interpret correctly, it would mean that we entrust the MP, a role of "missi dominici" of the republic. He does represent the republic on the field and that's how I understand this sentence. Is this the way it should be read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I'm personally not familiar with the role of "missi dominici." In order to answer your question fully, if that could be explained to me. That's how it appears on the transcript, "missi dominici."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Hanson, would that mean that the MP, that in your understanding that the MP is the representative of the republic vis-a-vis the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreter, for the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my understanding, bearing in mind that we know that deputies of the Assembly were to be members of the Crisis Staff and the Crisis Staffs become the municipal authorities and do so, as we saw from the Assembly discussions in February and March, looking to the Assembly for instructions about how to set up a state because the whole Bosnian Serb state is being created at this point, and they see the Assembly as one of the engines -- one of the core organs of the state and also the engine for the establishment of this state. And since they are creating their own state, they are giving themselves authority, and the Assembly they see as the supreme authority. And they go to the municipalities as members of the Crisis Staffs and as representatives of the republican authorities. We also saw that in the discussion on republican commissioners in November 1992 where they say it doesn't matter whether it's a commissioner or a deputy, what matters is the psychological effect. Someone coming to the municipalities is seen as representing, in that passage, the republican organs in general. But specifically, I tied that here to their role on Crisis Staffs and to the role in the Assembly in the establishment of the Bosnian Serb state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sorry, Your Honour. I notice the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have this document in front of us, I would have one additional question, especially on the speech of Mr. Mijatovic. In the beginning of his speech, and that's on page 57, he refers to discussions in the club sessions, which are announced. He says: "We are told that we are going to have a club session after the first two points, probably meaning most of us; that it would be better if we discuss the issues that bother us calmly among us without making them public." I noticed that -- I hope you'll forgive me that I do not remember exactly the moment when you said this, I remember that you said something about after the break, or something like that. Was this a pattern that part of the problems were discussed in public and that sometimes everyone thought it better to not publicly discuss matters either to reach agreement or for whatever reason? Is that something you came across more than on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall Krajisnik's speech on the 24th of March, 1992, saying a single method will be applied. I think we'll hear more about it in the form of instructions at the Deputies' Club. He does not say there explicitly, so as not to discuss it in public, but he is referring to the Deputies' Club as another way of communicating information. We also see, in general, that the Deputies' Club I think tended to meet before each Assembly session there would be a meeting. And there was, to the best of my knowledge, not the same formal transcript made of those meetings. I am not aware, in the parts that I have read of the Assembly minutes, other explicit references to doing it without making them public, but I was reading the Assembly minutes more with an eye to discussions of the municipal level and not of the relationship between the Deputies' Club and the Assembly. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just re-reading your answer. So you say that in general, the Deputies' Club tended to meet before each Assembly session --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding. Again, I have to repeat, I did not prepare and really fix in my mind the details of the republican procedures for this presentation. But that's my understanding, in general, of my study of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would those who would have access to those Deputies' Club meetings, would they have majority or a minority in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it was much the same body. I'm not sure of the make-up of the Deputies' Club, but I believe it was the SDS deputies, which is almost the entire Assembly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before I give you an opportunity to proceed, perhaps it would be wise, since footnote 83 is on my mind, although not all the time, perhaps we could have the clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I found the documents in question, and they are two different documents. The error -- oh, footnote 83, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have two issues.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Footnote 83 and footnote -- let me see, footnote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- footnote 68. Yes, perhaps we first deal with 68 because we specifically put that question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They are two different documents. The error is in my description of the second document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The footnote refers to the relationship of the regional Crisis Staffs in the RS state system. And the -- just to show you the first document, that is, 00835801, to show that it's quite clearly what I say it is, it is the declaration of a state of war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- on the Serbian Autonomous Region of Birac. So that is as described the footnote and it is cited as the National Defence Council of the RS. The error is in the description of the second document, which is listed in the footnote as 00835773, but that it's -- it's actually a three-page document and the relevant portion is on the last page, 00835775. It's a document by the Crisis Staff of Bratunac, which cites: "A decision of the National Security Council and a decision of the cell Birac Crisis Staff and a decision of the commissioner of the government of the Serbian Republic for Birac." And it is not as described in the footnote, my apologies, where the error crept in. But it is relevant in the text, describing the role of the regional Crisis Staffs in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it will give you some confidence that we even read every detail of the footnote to compare them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know the numbers better than I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when we have footnote -- so in the description, could we have -- I mean it would be a waste of paper. Could we have the proper description of that source given to us, because I think it does not appear in the list clearly, because if I look at footnote 68 in the -- well, let's say the database, then I have -- let me just have a look. 68 is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe there are four references to footnote 68, and the last one is on page 19 of the spreadsheet and it makes reference to a 6th May decision of the Bratunac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is the decision you wanted to refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have the description now, and that is presentation tab 310, at least that's what I see from my list. And that's presentation binder 5, tab 310, or master binder 5, tab 200. And I do see that it was already in evidence, is that correct, P57 and 57.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That having been clarified, we now move to footnote 83, the Ilijas request for manpower.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the footnote number again was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 83, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 83, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- 83 in the documents, yes. There is no error now that I see. I must have been -- my apologies. It is the document that I said it was. The error must have been in my simply reviewing quickly the documents. There are two, as I said, side by side that are quite similar, but in fact it is the correct ERN; there is no error. I was confused when reviewing, and I'm glad to report that it is correct, now that I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, having read it, it seems to be an invitation for paramilitaries to come to their assistance --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and issued by a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. There are two such invitations and they were right next to each other in the -- in the evidence record. And one is to one organisation and I had thought I had got the wrong organisation cited, but in fact the one cited is as described to the Serb volunteer guard. And I was confused, not when writing; I was confused later. My apologies for that -- for the waste of time and the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stewart, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, as a follow-up to Judge Hanoteau's question, I actually can't think of a better way of putting this point to you but with a very short slight anecdote. There was an English Member of Parliament at Westminster who in years gone by when he was criticised for not appearing very often in his constituency responded, he wouldn't be able to get away with it these days, but responded by saying, I am elected to represent Tunbridge Wells at Westminster and not Westminster in Tunbridge Wells. Now, I put to you that actually does encapsulate what is also the position here as far as the Serb Assembly is concerned, that the Assembly, and this was, with respect, I believe the Judge Hanoteau also was putting to you, that the Assembly members are elected to represent the people for the constituency or the district that elects them, and they are not elected to represent the government or any republican authority in their district.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputies that make up the Assembly -- that make up the Bosnian Serb Assembly were elected to the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia, and they set up this separate assembly which, as I said, played a crucial role in the formation of the Bosnian Serb state and the whole -- the Bosnian Serb authorities were defining that authority, the authority of the Assembly of the state as they created the state. And as we see, Karadzic said to the deputies, "You are members of the supreme organ of authority." So the special role of the Assembly in the formation of the Bosnian Serb state gave the deputies a role which they did not have in, for example, the British system.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I -- Ms. Hanson, we're not here to have a -- though it would be very interesting, no doubt, to have a seminar or a debate about political theory, practice, practice a bit more perhaps. But I have to put it to you -- well, you use the British example, the United Kingdom example. I would like to put it to you that in describing the Assembly as a supreme organ, that is entirely correct in this sense, that it's the legislature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a legislature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when it passes laws, those are the laws that have to be applied by the courts and have to be observed by the citizens. We'll leave aside the Republika Srpska/Bosnia element. But in Republika Srpska terms, that's the position, isn't it? It's the supreme organ because it passes the laws, and when it passes the laws, those are the laws, the courts have to apply the laws, and the citizens within Republika Srpska are expected and it is their civil duty -- civic duty to obey the laws. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in that sense it is very clear how and why the Assembly is described as the supreme organ?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Karadzic describes the assemblies as a supreme organ, he then goes on to discuss how the assemblymen should go to the municipalities and sit with the presidents of the municipalities and carry out -- implement the policies of the Assembly. That is the context of Karadzic's reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you talking about -- well, let's be clear which reference you are talking about then. There's one thing we can confidently agree upon is that Dr. Karadzic made a lot of speeches.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're talking about the Assembly Session on the 24th of March, 1992, aren't you, found at presentation tab 110, master tab 389. Is that correct? You --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is tab 110. If I can see it I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is as well, Ms. Hanson. Let's make sure that we're on the same hymn sheet here.
